pos: n. (Johannes Pistorius of Woerden, d. 1525, one of the first martyrs of the Dutch Reformation)
etymology: Latin Johannes, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Pistorius, a latinised form of Backer, a baker, from Latin pistor.
biblical_def: Johannes Pistorius — Jan de Bakker of Woerden — was a young priest of Holland who read Luther, came to the doctrine of free justification, resigned his benefice, married, and preached the gospel in his own town. He was arrested by the imperial authorities, examined at The Hague, and offered his life repeatedly if he would recant. He would not, and on 15 September 1525 he was degraded from the priesthood and burned at The Hague, the first Hollander to die for the evangelical faith. The contemporary accounts report that he sang psalms at the stake and that his fellow prisoners answered him from their cell windows as he passed, which is the detail that fixed him in the Dutch memory. Erasmus, who knew of the case, wrote of it with evident discomfort. The Dutch Reformation, which would run for a century and a half through hedge-preaching, iconoclasm, war and a national synod, begins with a married priest from Woerden singing on his way to a fire. “for I am ready not to be bound only, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus” (Act 21:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to degrade as to deprive of office or dignity, and martyrdom as the suffering of death on account of adherence to the faith.
webster_full: DEGRA'DE, v. To reduce from a higher to a lower rank; to deprive of office or dignity.
MAR'TYRDOM, n. The death of a martyr; the suffering of death on account of adherence to the Christian faith.
BEN'EFICE, n. In church affairs, an ecclesiastical living; a church endowed with a revenue.
STAKE, n. The post to which one condemned to be burnt is bound.
scriptures: Then Paul answered, What mean ye to weep and to break mine heart? for I am ready not to be bound only, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.
Php 1:21
For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
For I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand.
Rev 20:4

And I saw thrones, and they sat upon them, and judgment was given unto them: and I saw the souls of them that were beheaded for the witness of Jesus, and for the word of God, and which had not worshipped the beast, neither his image, neither had received his mark upon their foreheads, or in their hands; and they lived and reigned with Christ a thousand years.
corruption_summary: Jan de Bakker of Woerden, burned at The Hague in 1525, singing.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a general one applied to all these early deaths: that the first evangelicals were punished as disturbers of civil order rather than for doctrine, so the religious question is incidental. The record of Pistorius's examination is specific. He was asked whether the mass is a sacrifice for the living and the dead, whether a priest may marry, and whether a man is justified by faith alone, and it was his answers that killed him.

The principle to recover is that a readiness to die is not a heroic temperament but a settled valuation, and the New Testament states it as an arithmetic rather than an emotion: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Php 1:21). Paul's reply to the friends who wept over him at Caesarea is the same thing in the imperative mood: “What mean ye to weep and to break mine heart?” (Act 21:13).

“the souls of them that were beheaded for the witness of Jesus” (Rev 20:4) — where the Dutch Reformation begins.

pos: n. (Cornelis Cooltuyn, 1526–1567, preacher at Alkmaar and Emden, called the father of the Dutch Reformation)
etymology: Latin Cornelius, a Roman gens name; Cooltuyn, Dutch for cabbage-garden, a family name from a holding.
biblical_def: Cornelis Cooltuyn was a priest of Alkmaar in North Holland who came to the evangelical faith and preached it from his own pulpit in Dutch, plainly, for several years before the authorities moved against him. In 1557 he fled to Emden, the East Frisian port that was the mother city of the Dutch Reformation in exile, and ministered there until his death in 1567. His book Het Evangelie der Armen — the Gospel of the Poor — published in 1559, is one of the earliest Dutch evangelical works written for ordinary readers rather than for scholars; it sets out justification by faith in the language of market and farm, and it circulated widely in the Netherlands in a form that could be hidden in a pocket. Later Dutch writers gave him the name of the father of their Reformation, meaning not that he founded it but that he first put it into Dutch for the Dutch poor. “he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor” (Luk 4:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the poor as those who have little property, and the gospel as the good tidings of salvation by Christ.
webster_full: POOR, a. Wholly destitute of property, or not having property sufficient for a comfortable subsistence.
GOS'PEL, n. The good tidings of salvation by Christ; the history of the life and death of Christ.
TRACT, n. A small book or pamphlet; a short treatise.
VERNAC'ULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth.
scriptures: Luk 4:18

The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised,
Mat 11:5
The blind receive their sight, and the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have the gospel preached to them.
Jam 2:5
Hearken, my beloved brethren, Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he hath promised to them that love him?
Luk 6:20
And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said, Blessed be ye poor: for yours is the kingdom of God.
corruption_summary: The Alkmaar priest who wrote the Gospel of the Poor in plain Dutch.
corruption_paragraphs: A modern reading of a title like Het Evangelie der Armen immediately hears liberation theology: the gospel as the poor's charter against the rich, salvation as social deliverance. Cooltuyn's book does not say that, and the misreading costs the poor the thing he was giving them. His argument is that the gospel is free, that it therefore requires no learning, no money for masses and no priestly mediation, and that a labourer may have it as completely as a bishop.

The principle to recover is that God's preference for the poor is real and is a preference in calling rather than a political programme: “Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he hath promised to them that love him?” (Jam 2:5). The Lord makes preaching to the poor the proof of his own commission and sets it last in the list, as the climax: “and the poor have the gospel preached to them” (Mat 11:5).

pos: n. (Johannes Anastasius Veluanus, c. 1520–1570, author of Der Leken Wechwyser, the first Protestant theology in Dutch)
etymology: A pen-name: Anastasius, from Greek anastasis, resurrection; Veluanus, of the Veluwe in Gelderland. His name was Jan Gerritsz Versteghe.
biblical_def: Johannes Anastasius Veluanus was the pen-name of Jan Gerritsz Versteghe, parish priest of Garderen on the Veluwe, who preached the evangelical faith to his own flock and was arrested in 1550. During more than three years in prison at Arnhem he wrote Der Leken Wechwyser — the Layman's Wayfinder — published in 1554, the first systematic treatment of Protestant doctrine composed in Dutch for Dutch readers. It handles God, man, sin, Christ, justification, the sacraments and the Christian life in order, in a homely style aimed at people with no Latin, and it went through many editions and shaped the religious vocabulary of the Dutch Reformation; on the Lord's Supper and on predestination it is closer to Melanchthon than to Geneva, which later Dutch Reformed writers noted and corrected. He recanted under pressure to get out of prison, afterwards repudiated the recantation, fled, and ministered at Bentheim and Haarlem until his death. “So that my bonds in Christ are manifest in all the palace” (Php 1:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a wayfinder as a guide, and a system as a regular method or order of principles reduced to a whole.
webster_full: SYS'TEM, n. An assemblage of things adjusted into a regular whole; a regular method or order.
GUIDE, n. A person who leads or directs another in his way or course; a director; a regulator.
LA'YMAN, n. One of the people, as distinct from the clergy; a man not in orders.
BONDS, n. Imprisonment; captivity; chains.
scriptures: Php 1:13
So that my bonds in Christ are manifest in all the palace, and in all other places;
Php 1:14
And many of the brethren in the Lord, waxing confident by my bonds, are much more bold to speak the word without fear.
And Paul dwelt two whole years in his own hired house, and received all that came in unto him,
Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching those things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ, with all confidence, no man forbidding him.
corruption_summary: Three years in Arnhem prison, and the first Dutch book of systematic divinity.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a confessional one: because the Wechwyser is not Reformed at every point, Dutch Reformed historiography has sometimes handled Veluanus as a transitional embarrassment rather than as the man who first made it possible to discuss these doctrines in Dutch at all. The dictionary names his departures from the Reformed position and keeps the debt.

The principle to recover is that imprisonment has repeatedly been the most productive condition of the church's writers, and Scripture presents this as a providence rather than an irony: “And many of the brethren in the Lord, waxing confident by my bonds, are much more bold to speak the word without fear” (Php 1:14). Luke ends Acts with Paul under guard and still at work: “Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching those things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ, with all confidence” (Act 28:31).

Greek praitorion (G4232) — the praetorium, the palace; Philippians 1:13.

Greek misthoma (G3410) — a hired dwelling; Acts 28:30.

“waxing confident by my bonds, are much more bold to speak the word without fear” (Php 1:14) — the Layman's Wayfinder.
“Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching those things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ” (Act 28:31) — a book written under guard.

pos: n. (Gellius Faber de Bouma, c. 1490–1564, minister at Emden, controversialist against the Anabaptists)
etymology: Frisian Gellius, from the Roman gens name; Faber, Latin for smith, latinising his family name Smit, with de Bouma for his Frisian origin.
biblical_def: Gellius Faber de Bouma was a Frisian priest who came over to the Reformation and from 1537 was a minister at Emden, the East Frisian city that sheltered the Dutch Reformed in exile and became their organising centre. He worked there alongside John a Lasco when a Lasco was superintendent of the East Frisian church, and he is chiefly remembered for the controversy he had to conduct. Emden lay at the heart of the Anabaptist movement in the Low Countries, and in 1552 Faber published a treatise defending the baptism of infants and the lawfulness of the magistracy and the ministerial office against the Anabaptist teachers. Menno Simons answered it the following year in his Reply to Gellius Faber, which is the longest and most autobiographical of Menno's writings and would hardly exist without Faber's book. The dictionary holds the Reformed side of that exchange and notes what it cost him: he argued for a generation with men whose sufferings under Rome had been as heavy as his own. “For the promise is unto you, and to your children” (Act 2:39).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an Anabaptist as one who holds the baptism of infants to be unlawful, and a covenant as a mutual agreement, here of God with men.
webster_full: ANABAP'TIST, n. One who holds the baptism of infants to be unlawful and void, and insists on rebaptism.
COV'ENANT, n. A mutual agreement; in theology, the covenant of grace made with man in Christ.
CIRCUMCI'SION, n. The act of cutting off the prepuce; the sign of the Abrahamic covenant.
CONTROVER'SY, n. Dispute; debate; agitation of contrary opinions.
scriptures: Act 2:39
For the promise is unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off, even as many as the Lord our God shall call.
Gen 17:7
And I will establish my covenant between me and thee and thy seed after thee in their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee.
Col 2:11
In whom also ye are circumcised with the circumcision made without hands, in putting off the body of the sins of the flesh by the circumcision of Christ:
Col 2:12
Buried with him in baptism, wherein also ye are risen with him through the faith of the operation of God, who hath raised him from the dead.
corruption_summary: The Emden minister whose book on infant baptism Menno Simons answered.
corruption_paragraphs: The Anabaptist objection Faber answered is the one still made: that baptism presupposes a credible profession, that the New Testament records no infant baptism, and that a church of the baptised must therefore be a church of professors. The Reformed answer he gave is that the covenant sign has always been administered to the seed of believers, that the New Testament nowhere narrows the covenant promise, and that the burden lies on those who would exclude the children whom God had expressly included.

The principle to recover is the continuity of the covenant and of its sign. The promise to Abraham is stated with the children in it — “to be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee” (Gen 17:7) — and Peter repeats the form of words on the day of Pentecost without narrowing it: “For the promise is unto you, and to your children” (Act 2:39). Paul sets baptism in the place circumcision held: “Buried with him in baptism” (Col 2:12).

roots_lines: Greek epaggelia (G1860) — a promise, an announcement; Acts 2:39.
Greek proskaleomai (G4341) — to call to oneself, summon; Acts 2:39.

Hebrew berith (H1285) — a covenant, league; Genesis 17:7.
Greek sunthapto (G4916) — to bury together with; Colossians 2:12.

“to be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee” (Gen 17:7) — the covenant Menno would narrow.
“Buried with him in baptism” (Col 2:12) — the sign set in circumcision's place.

pos: n. (Albert Hardenberg, c. 1510–1574, preacher at Bremen, driven out over the Lord's Supper)
etymology: German Albert, noble and bright, from Germanic athal and beraht; Hardenberg, a place in Overijssel.
biblical_def: Albert Hardenberg was a Dutchman of Hardenberg in Overijssel, educated at Groningen and Louvain, a monk of the Adwert abbey where he met the humanist circle, and a friend of John a Lasco and of Melanchthon. From 1547 he was cathedral preacher at Bremen, and there he became the centre of the longest and most damaging of the German sacramental quarrels. Hardenberg held the Reformed doctrine of Christ's spiritual presence to faith and denied the bodily presence in the elements; the strict Lutheran ministers of Bremen and the Lower Saxon cities pressed him for a decade, colloquies were held, Melanchthon was appealed to and answered too mildly to satisfy anyone, and in 1561 the city deposed and banished him. He spent his last years at Emden and Sengwarden. It is a hard entry to write without bitterness: a man was driven from a Protestant city by Protestants for holding what Geneva, Zurich and Heidelberg all confessed. “It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing” (Joh 6:63).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a colloquy as a conference or mutual discourse, and to quicken as to make alive, to vivify.
webster_full: COL'LOQUY, n. Conversation; mutual discourse of two or more; a conference.
QUICK'EN, v. To make alive; to vivify; to revive or resuscitate, as from death.
SPIR'ITUAL, a. Consisting of spirit; not material; pertaining to the mind or to the renewed nature.
DEPO'SE, v. To divest of office; to deprive of ministry; to degrade.
scriptures: Joh 6:63
It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life.
For we being many are one bread, and one body: for we are all partakers of that one bread.
But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup.
Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water.
corruption_summary: The Bremen preacher banished by Protestants for the Reformed doctrine of the Supper.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern verdict on the whole affair: that the sacramental controversies were a scandal and both parties were at fault for prosecuting them, from which it follows that the right course is to leave the question open. The Hardenberg case shows why that course is not available. Both sides thought the question concerned the person of Christ and the nature of the believer's union with him, and on that they were right; a church that declines to answer it has not kept the peace but abandoned the subject.

The principle to recover is the Reformed doctrine itself, which is neither a bare memorial nor a bodily presence in the bread: the believer truly feeds on Christ, by the Spirit, through faith. The Lord sets the terms in the same discourse that is usually quoted against them: “It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life” (Joh 6:63). Paul makes the communion a real participation: “for we are all partakers of that one bread” (1Co 10:17).

pos: n. (Hermannus Moded, c. 1520–1603, hedge-preacher of the Netherlands, implicated in the image-breaking of 1566)
etymology: German Herman, army-man, from Germanic hari and man; Moded, a grecising of his family name Strijcker, a smoother or stroker.
biblical_def: Hermannus Moded was a Zwolle man, trained at Geneva, and the most inflammatory of the preachers of the Dutch hagepreken — the hedge-sermons of 1566, held in open fields outside the walls because the cities were closed to them, drawing crowds of many thousands under armed guard. He preached at Antwerp in that summer, and when the image-breaking broke out in August and ran through the Low Countries — altars torn down, statues smashed, church furniture burnt in hundreds of buildings — his preaching was held by the authorities, and by some of his own colleagues, to have set it off. He denied directing it. He fled at Alva's coming, served congregations in exile, returned with Orange, and ministered until 1603. The dictionary affirms the Second Commandment and declines to approve the Beeldenstorm: images are to be removed by lawful authority after instruction, not by crowds, and what happened in 1566 cost the Reformed cause in the Netherlands the sympathy of many who agreed with its doctrine. “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exo 20:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an iconoclast as a breaker of images, and a graven image as an idol formed by carving.
webster_full: ICON'OCLAST, n. A breaker or destroyer of images; one who opposes the worship of images.
GRA'VEN, pp. Carved; engraved; a graven image, an idol formed by carving.
TU'MULT, n. The commotion, disturbance or agitation of a multitude; a riot.
ZEAL, n. Passionate ardour in the pursuit of anything; ardour in the pursuit of what one believes right.
scriptures: Exo 20:4
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
Exo 20:5

Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;
Isa 42:8
I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images.
For ye have brought hither these men, which are neither robbers of churches, nor yet blasphemers of your goddess.
corruption_summary: The hedge-preacher of 1566, and the image-breaking the dictionary will not approve.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors meet over the Beeldenstorm. Roman and secular accounts use it to tar the Reformed cause as mob vandalism indifferent to beauty, and a strand of Protestant writing celebrates it as righteous zeal against idolatry. The dictionary accepts neither. The Second Commandment stands, and the images in those churches were objects of worship and rightly to be removed; a crowd with hammers is not the lawful means, and Paul's own practice at Ephesus is the standing rebuke — the town clerk could say of the apostolic company that they were “neither robbers of churches, nor yet blasphemers of your goddess” (Act 19:37).

The principle to recover is that zeal for a true commandment must still submit to a lawful order. The command itself is absolute — “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exo 20:4) — and the ground is God's own jealousy for his honour: “my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images” (Isa 42:8). That God is jealous does not make every hand that smashes a statue his instrument.

Hebrew temunah (H8544) — a likeness, form, similitude; Exodus 20:4.

Hebrew kabod (H3519) — glory, honour, weight; Isaiah 42:8.

“my glory will I not give to another” (Isa 42:8) — why the images had to go.

pos: n. (Caspar van der Heyden, 1530–1586, minister at Antwerp and Frankenthal, organiser of the Synod of Emden)
etymology: German Caspar, from Persian through Latin, a treasurer; van der Heyden, of the heath.
biblical_def: Caspar van der Heyden was a Mechelen man, a tailor by trade before he was a minister, trained in exile, and one of the chief builders of the Dutch Reformed church as an institution. He served the congregation at Antwerp through the perilous years of the 1560s, fled to the Palatinate, ministered to the Dutch refugees at Frankenthal, and was repeatedly at the centre of the gatherings that gave the scattered churches a constitution. He translated the Heidelberg Catechism into Dutch, and at the Synod of Emden in October 1571 — held in exile, by delegates from congregations under the cross, with no state behind it — he was among those who drew up the church order that set the Belgic Confession and the Heidelberg Catechism as the standards of the Dutch churches and established the presbyterian courts of consistory, classis and synod. That order, revised at Dort in 1618, governs Reformed churches on several continents still. “And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a synod as a council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion, and a classis as an inferior judicatory of elders.
webster_full: SYN'OD, n. A council or meeting of ecclesiastical persons to consult on matters of religion.
CLAS'SIS, n. In the Reformed churches, an assembly of the ministers and elders of several churches.
CHURCH ORDER, The constitution and rules by which a church governs itself.
CONFU'SION, n. Disorder; irregularity; want of order or arrangement.
scriptures: Act 15:6
And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.
For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things;
For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints.
Eph 4:16

From whom the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part, maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love.
corruption_summary: The tailor-turned-minister who helped draw the Dutch church order at Emden in 1571.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a widespread modern impatience with church order as institutional clutter obstructing the Spirit's freedom. The Synod of Emden answers it by its circumstances. These were congregations meeting in cellars and fields with their ministers under sentence of death, and what they did with their one chance to confer was to write a constitution, because they had learned that a church without courts cannot discipline, cannot ordain, and cannot survive a generation.

The principle to recover is that the apostolic church met in council to settle a disputed question and issued a decision binding on the churches: “And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6). The decree that followed claims the Spirit's own concurrence in an assembly's judgment — “For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us” (Act 15:28) — and Paul grounds order in the character of God: “For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace” (1Co 14:33).

Greek eidon, to see, consider; logos (G3056) — a matter, account; Acts 15:6.
Greek epitithemi (G2007) — to lay upon, impose; Acts 15:28.
Greek akatastasia (G181) — disorder, confusion, tumult; 1 Corinthians 14:33.
Greek sunarmologeo (G4883) — to fit or frame together; Ephesians 4:16.

“For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us” (Act 15:28) — a synod's warrant.
“For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace” (1Co 14:33) — why churches under the cross wrote a constitution.

pos: n. (Petrus Dathenus, c. 1531–1588, Flemish minister, author of the Dutch metrical psalter of 1566)
etymology: Latin Petrus, from Greek petros, a stone; Dathenus, a latinised form of Pieter Datheen, from his birthplace Cassel in Flanders.
biblical_def: Petrus Dathenus was a Flemish Carmelite who left his order for the Reformation and became one of the most energetic and least comfortable men in the Dutch church. He ministered to refugee congregations at London, Frankfurt and Frankenthal, where the Elector Palatine gave the Flemish exiles a town; he was moderator of the Synod of Emden in 1571; and he was repeatedly in the thick of the politics of the revolt, where his vehemence at Ghent in 1578 against toleration for Rome made him enemies and eventually, after a bitter quarrel, brought his deposition. His lasting work is the psalter. In 1566 he published a Dutch metrical version of all one hundred and fifty psalms, fitted to the Genevan tunes, together with his Dutch translation of the Heidelberg Catechism and a liturgy; the Dutch Reformed churches sang Dathenus for two hundred and seven years, until 1773. “Sing unto the LORD a new song, and his praise in the congregation of saints” (Psa 149:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a psalter as the book of Psalms, and a liturgy as a form of prayers used in public worship.
webster_full: PSAL'TER, n. The book of Psalms; a psalm-book for singing in public worship.
LIT'URGY, n. A form of prayers and ceremonial observances used in the public worship of God.
ME'TRE, n. The arrangement of a certain number of syllables in a certain order; measure; verse.
CON'GREGATION, n. An assembly of persons met for the worship of God.
scriptures: Praise ye the LORD. Sing unto the LORD a new song, and his praise in the congregation of saints.
Sing unto him, sing psalms unto him, talk ye of all his wondrous works.
Psa 30:4
Sing unto the LORD, O ye saints of his, and give thanks at the remembrance of his holiness.
Deu 6:6
And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart:
corruption_summary: The Dutch psalter the churches sang for two hundred and seven years.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the sentimental treatment of a long-serving psalter as sacred in itself. Dathenus's Dutch was rough even by the standards of his own century and grew steadily harder to sing as the language moved; the churches kept it for two centuries partly from reverence and partly from inertia, and the 1773 revision was overdue when it came. A version is a servant and may be retired.

The principle to recover is that the congregation is commanded to sing and that the matter of its singing is largely given to it already: “Sing unto the LORD a new song, and his praise in the congregation of saints” (Psa 149:1). The command includes speaking of God's works as well as singing them — “Sing unto him, sing psalms unto him, talk ye of all his wondrous works” (1Ch 16:9) — and a metrical psalter is simply the means by which a people who cannot read can carry the Psalms in their memory.

“these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart” (Deu 6:6) — what a metrical psalter is for.

pos: n. (Jean Taffin, 1529–1602, court preacher to William of Orange, author of The Marks of the Children of God)
etymology: French Jean, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Taffin, a Walloon family name of Tournai.
biblical_def: Jean Taffin was a Walloon of Tournai who studied under Calvin and Beza, served the Reformed congregations of Antwerp and Metz, and became court preacher to William of Orange and afterwards to his son Maurice, with a long ministry at Haarlem and Amsterdam. He stood at the Synod of Emden and in the counsels of the young Dutch church. His book Des marques des enfans de Dieu et des consolations en leurs afflictions, published in 1586, is the first substantial work of experiential Reformed piety written for the Dutch churches: it sets out the marks by which a believer may know himself a child of God, and the comforts proper to a people under persecution, and it went through many editions in French and Dutch. It is the headwater of the tradition that became the Nadere Reformatie, the Dutch Second Reformation of Teellinck, Voetius and Lodenstein. A court preacher who wrote for frightened people about assurance did more lasting work than any of his political errands. “The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God” (Rom 8:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines assurance as firm persuasion, full confidence, and a mark as a token or evidence by which anything is known.
webster_full: ASSU'RANCE, n. Firm persuasion; full confidence or trust; freedom from doubt; certain expectation.
MARK, n. A visible sign or impression; a token; evidence; whatever serves to designate.
CONSOLA'TION, n. Comfort; alleviation of misery or distress of mind.
EXPE'RIENCE, n. Trial; proof by trial; knowledge gained by actual trial or practice.
scriptures: Rom 8:16
The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God:
We know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren. He that loveth not his brother abideth in death.
These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life, and that ye may believe on the name of the Son of God.
Wherefore the rather, brethren, give diligence to make your calling and election sure: for if ye do these things, ye shall never fall:
corruption_summary: The headwater of Dutch experiential piety, written for a persecuted people.
corruption_paragraphs: Taffin's subject has been corrupted in two opposite directions since. One is the therapeutic assurance of modern religion, in which a believer is told never to examine himself at all because doubt is unhealthy, so that the marks Taffin set out are dismissed as morbid introspection. The other is the opposite excess within the very tradition he founded, where the marks hardened into a lengthy inventory that few dared claim and assurance became the rare attainment of the aged.

The principle to recover is Taffin's own balance, which is the New Testament's. Assurance is the Spirit's own testimony and not a conclusion a man argues himself into: “The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God” (Rom 8:16). It is also to be tested by evidence that can be looked for — “We know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren” (1Jo 3:14) — and John writes expressly so that believers may have it: “that ye may know that ye have eternal life” (1Jo 5:13).

pos: n. (Philips van Marnix, Lord of Saint-Aldegonde, 1540–1598, statesman, satirist and translator of the Dutch revolt)
etymology: Greek Philippos, lover of horses; Marnix, a family of Savoyard origin; Saint-Aldegonde, his seigneury in Hainaut.
biblical_def: Philips van Marnix, Lord of Saint-Aldegonde, was a nobleman of Brussels who studied at Geneva under Calvin and Beza and returned to become William of Orange's closest counsellor and the pen of the Dutch revolt. He drafted the Compromise of the Nobles in 1565, argued the Protestant case at the Diet of Worms in 1578, negotiated at every stage, served as burgomaster of Antwerp and surrendered the city to Parma after a thirteen-month siege, for which he was blamed for the rest of his life. He is credited with the Wilhelmus, the song of the revolt that is now the Dutch national anthem, and he wrote the Byencorf der Heilige Roomsche Kercke, a satire on the Roman church in the voice of a credulous defender of it, which was one of the most effective polemics of the century. In his last years the States of Holland commissioned him to translate the Bible from the Hebrew and Greek into Dutch; he had finished Genesis when he died. A layman who gave his people a confession, an anthem and the beginning of a Bible. “every one with one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other hand held a weapon” (Neh 4:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a satire as a discourse exposing vice or folly, and a statesman as a man versed in the arts of government.
webster_full: SAT'IRE, n. A discourse or poem in which wickedness or folly is exposed with severity; keen reproach.
STATES'MAN, n. A man versed in the arts of government; one eminent for political abilities.
ANTHEM, n. A hymn sung in alternate parts; a sacred song or a national song of praise.
SEIGN'IORY, n. A lordship; the territory of a lord; a manor.
scriptures: Neh 4:17
They which builded on the wall, and they that bare burdens, with those that laded, every one with one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other hand held a weapon.
Dan 1:17
As for these four children, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom: and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams.
Jer 1:10
See, I have this day set thee over the nations and over the kingdoms, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant.
Eph 6:17
And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God:
corruption_summary: Orange's counsellor, author of the Beehive and of the Wilhelmus, Bible translator at the last.
corruption_paragraphs: Marnix is now remembered as a statesman and a poet, with the theology that drove him treated as the idiom of his age. It was the whole substance. He studied under Calvin, he wrote the Beehive because he believed the Roman church had corrupted the gospel, he defended the Reformed confession at Worms against his own political interest, and he spent his last strength on Genesis in Dutch. A secular reading of such a life has to discard most of its evidence to reach its conclusion.

The principle to recover is that public service and the labour of the word belong together in a Christian commonwealth, and Nehemiah is the pattern: the builders worked with one hand and held a weapon in the other, and the work was the city of God. “every one with one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other hand held a weapon” (Neh 4:17). The weapon Paul names for such men is the one Marnix ended with: “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph 6:17).
